### The Icon of Democracy: How Corazon Aquino Led a Peaceful Revolution

On August 21, 1983, a single gunshot on the tarmac of Manila International Airport altered the course of Philippine history. Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr., the primary political rival of dictator Ferdinand Marcos, was assassinated upon returning from exile. Out of this tragedy emerged an unlikely champion of freedom: Ninoy’s grieving widow, Corazon "Cory" Aquino. A self-described "simple housewife" with no prior political experience, Cory was thrust into the international spotlight. Over the next three years, her quiet resolve transformed national grief into a formidable movement, ultimately dismantling two decades of authoritarian rule through the power of peaceful resistance.

#### The Rise of a Reluctant Leader
By the mid-1980s, the Philippines was reeling under the oppressive weight of Ferdinand Marcos’s regime. Declared in 1972, Martial Law had dismantled democratic institutions, silenced the free press, and resulted in widespread human rights abuses, including the torture, disappearance, and imprisonment of political dissidents. Compounding the political tyranny was a collapsing economy, ravaged by corruption and the plunder of state coffers by Marcos and his cronies.

Following Ninoy’s murder, public outrage reached a boiling point. The Philippine opposition, historically fragmented, needed a unifying figurehead to challenge the regime. They found it in Cory Aquino. Relying on her moral authority and untainted reputation, she reluctantly accepted the mantle of leadership. 

In late 1985, seeking to reassert his legitimacy amid growing domestic and international pressure, Marcos called a "snap" presidential election for February 1986. Cory launched a nation-spanning campaign, adopting the color yellow—symbolic of the welcome ribbons tied for Ninoy’s expected return—as her movement’s trademark. Despite systemic voter intimidation, widespread disenfranchisement, and blatant fraud by the government-controlled Commission on Elections (COMELEC), Aquino’s supporters stood firm. When Marcos prematurely declared himself the winner, the nation refused to accept the stolen result.

#### The People Power Revolution (EDSA)
The crisis reached its peak in late February 1986, when key military leaders, including Defense Minister Juan Ponce Enrile and Vice Chief of Staff General Fidel Ramos, withdrew their support from Marcos and barricaded themselves inside military camps along Epifanio de los Santos Avenue (EDSA), the main arterial road of metro Manila.

Recognizing the imminent danger of a bloody military crackdown, the Roman Catholic Church played a decisive, historic role. Cardinal Jaime Sin, the Archbishop of Manila, broadcast a passionate appeal over Catholic radio, urging everyday citizens to take to the streets to protect the rebel soldiers and demand Marcos's resignation. 

What followed was the historic "People Power Revolution." Over the course of four days, more than two million unarmed Filipino citizens—nuns, priests, students, families, and workers—flooded EDSA. Armed only with rosaries, flowers, food, and overwhelming courage, civilians stood directly in front of armed troops, armored personnel carriers, and tanks. Faced with the peaceful resistance of their own people, many soldiers refused orders to fire and instead joined the crowd. The nonviolent movement succeeded in completely paralyzing the regime’s military machine.

#### A New Era for the Philippines
On February 25, 1986, Cory Aquino was officially sworn in as the 11th President of the Philippines, becoming the nation’s first female head of state and the first in Asia. Realizing he had lost the support of both his military and his primary international ally, the United States, Ferdinand Marcos and his family fled into exile in Hawaii later that evening.

Aquino’s presidency was defined by the arduous task of restoring democracy to a shattered nation. She immediately dismantled the apparatus of the dictatorship, establishing a revolutionary government to swift-track reforms. In 1987, her administration promulgated a new constitution that reinstated a bicameral legislature, restored full civil liberties, established strict limits on presidential power, and placed safeguards against future declarations of Martial Law. 

While her six-year term was beset by massive challenges—including multiple violent coup attempts by disgruntled military factions, natural disasters, and persistent economic difficulties—Aquino successfully guided the nation back to constitutional governance. In 1992, adhering strictly to the constitutional limits she helped create, she stepped down, facilitating a peaceful transfer of power to her democratically elected successor, Fidel Ramos.

#### Legacy and Passing
After leaving office, Aquino remained a moral compass for the nation. She consistently used her platform to speak out against political corruption, defend democratic institutions, and mentor a new generation of leaders. 

On August 1, 2009, Corazon Aquino passed away at the age of 76 following a battle with colon cancer. Her death sparked a wave of nationwide mourning reminiscent of the 1986 revolution. Millions of Filipinos took to the streets once more, wearing yellow to honor the woman who had helped restore their freedom.

Corazon Aquino’s legacy extends far beyond the borders of the Philippines. By proving that a entrenched dictatorship could be peacefully defeated through faith, unity, and civilian courage, she provided a global blueprint for nonviolent movement building. Today, she is remembered worldwide as the "Mother of Asian Democracy"—a testament to how humility and moral conviction can overcome tyrant rule.

Her family announced that she died of cardiorespiratory arrest after a yearlong battle with colon cancer. 

In response to her passing, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo declared a 10-day period of national mourning, praising Mrs. Aquino for guiding the nation through one of its darkest chapters. "Cory Aquino led a revolution that restored democracy and the rule of law to our nation at a time of great peril," Arroyo said in a statement from an official visit to the United States. 

Mrs. Aquino’s unlikely transformation from a self-described "ordinary housewife" into a global icon of democracy began with a personal tragedy. For decades, she had remained in the background of her husband, Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Jr., the charismatic senator who was the chief political rival to Ferdinand Marcos.

Plunged into the political spotlight, Mrs. Aquino became the unyielding moral voice of a shattered opposition. 

Dressed in her signature yellow—the color inspired by the song "Tie a Yellow Ribbon Round the Ole Oak Tree," which supporters used to welcome her husband home—Mrs. Aquino ran against Marcos in the fraudulent February 1986 snap presidential election. When Marcos declared himself the victor despite blatant vote-tampering and violence, Mrs. Aquino called for civil disobedience. 

Her call sparked the historic "People Power" Revolution. Within days, Marcos fled into exile in Hawaii, and on February 25, 1986, Mrs. Aquino was sworn in as the 11th President of the Philippines, becoming the first woman to hold the office in Asia.

# Corazon Aquino, democracy icon and first female Philippine president, dies at 76

**By CNN Staff**  
Updated 0415 GMT (1215 HKT) August 1, 2009

**MANILA, Philippines (CNN) —** Corazon Aquino, the soft-spoken democracy icon who swept away decades of dictatorship in the Philippines to become the country’s first female president, died early Saturday following a battle with colon cancer, her family announced. She was 76.

Aquino passed away at 3:18 a.m. local time (1918 GMT Friday) at the Makati Medical Center in Manila due to cardiorespiratory arrest, according to her son, Sen. Benigno "Noynoy" Aquino III.

"Our mother peacefully passed away... She would have wanted to thank each and every one of you for all the prayers and continuous love and support," her son told reporters gathered outside the hospital.

Aquino was diagnosed with stage-four colon cancer in March 2008 and had been hospitalized for the past month as her condition deteriorated. 

Reacting to the news, Philippine President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo declared a 10-day period of national mourning. Speaking from the United States during an official visit, Arroyo praised Aquino as a national treasure.

"Aquino led a revolution that restored democracy and the rule of law to our nation at a time of great peril," Arroyo said in a statement. "The nation mourns the loss of a mother and a champion of freedom."

### A housewife turned political icon

Aquino, affectionately known to millions of Filipinos simply as "Tita Cory" (Auntie Cory), never sought a career in politics. For decades, she lived as a self-described "ordinary housewife," supporting her husband, Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Jr., a prominent senator and the fiercest political opponent of dictator Ferdinand Marcos.

Her life changed dramatically in August 1983 when her husband was assassinated on the tarmac of Manila’s international airport upon returning from political exile in the United States. 

Driven by grief and a sense of duty, Aquino emerged as the reluctant unifying figure for a fractured political opposition. Wearing her signature yellow—which became the symbol of the anti-Marcos movement—she challenged Marcos in a snap presidential election in February 1986.

When Marcos declared himself the winner despite widespread reports of voter fraud and intimidation, millions of Filipinos took to the streets in what became known as the "People Power Revolution." Armed only with flowers, rosaries, and yellow ribbons, citizens faced down military tanks on Manila’s main highway, Epifanio de los Santos Avenue (EDSA). 

The peaceful uprising forced Marcos into exile in Hawaii, and on February 25, 1986, Aquino was sworn in as the 11th president of the Philippines, becoming the first woman to hold the office.

### Leading a fragile democracy

Aquino’s presidency (1986–1992) was marked by monumental constitutional reform and persistent instability. 

Upon taking office, she promulgated a new constitution that placed strict limits on presidential terms to prevent the resurgence of authoritarian rule. She dismantled the apparatus of the Marcos regime, restored a free press, and reopened the nation's parliament.

### The 'People Power' Revolution

To millions of Filipinos and democracy advocates worldwide, Aquino will forever be remembered as the woman in yellow who stood up to authoritarian rule. 

Her journey to power was forged in tragedy. For years, Aquino was content living in the shadow of her husband, popular opposition leader Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Jr., a fierce critic of dictator Ferdinand Marcos. But when Ninoy was assassinated on the tarmac of the Manila airport upon returning from U.S. exile in August 1983, Cory was thrust into the political spotlight.

Wearing her signature yellow—inspired by the song "Tie a Yellow Ribbon Round the Ole Oak Tree"—she became the unified face of an enraged opposition. 

When Marcos called a "snap" presidential election in February 1986, Aquino ran against him. Following widespread reports of voting fraud and violence by the regime, the country reached a boiling point. Hundreds of thousands of civilians, urged by the influential Catholic Church, flooded Manila’s main highway, Epifanio de los Santos Avenue (EDSA). 

In what became known as the "People Power Revolution," unarmed citizens—nuns holding rosaries, students, and working-class families—confronted military tanks sent by Marcos. Soldiers refused to fire on the crowds. Within days, Marcos fled the country aboard a U.S. military aircraft, and on February 25, 1986, Aquino was sworn in as the first female president of the Philippines and of Asia.

Her peaceful revolution sent shockwaves across the world, providing a blueprint for nonviolent resistance that would echo years later during the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the Soviet bloc.

### A Turbulent Presidency

While Aquino’s rise to power was triumphant, her six-year term (1986–1992) was defined by intense political instability, economic hardship, and devastating natural disasters.

Inheriting a country burdened by billions of dollars in foreign debt and an economy crippled by decades of crony capitalism, Aquino worked swiftly to restore democratic institutions. She dissolved Marcos’s rubber-stamp parliament, promulgated a new constitution in 1987 that limited presidents to a single six-year term, and freed political prisoners.

However, her administration was relentlessly besieged from both the left and the right. She faced an active communist insurgency in the countryside and persistent threats from within her own military.

Between 1986 and 1989, Aquino survived at least seven military coup attempts led by renegade soldiers dissatisfied with her political concessions and economic policies. The deadliest attempt, in December 1989, nearly brought down her government and forced her to ask for military intervention from Washington.

Compounding the political crises were severe natural disasters. In July 1990, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake devastated central Luzon, followed in June 1991 by the cataclysmic eruption of Mount Pinatubo—one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the 20th century—which displaced hundreds of thousands of people and paralyzed the nation's economy.

### Complex Relations with Washington

Aquino’s presidency marked a critical turning point in the century-long relationship between the Philippines and its former colonial ruler, the United States. 

Initially, Washington had been a staunch ally of Ferdinand Marcos, viewing his regime as a crucial anti-communist stronghold during the Cold War. However, as Marcos’s legitimacy dissolved, U.S. policy shifted toward Aquino. 

In September 1986, just months after taking office, Aquino delivered a historic address to a joint session of the U.S. Congress. Dressed in her signature yellow, she called on the United States to help rebuild the democracy her people had fought to reclaim. Aquino resisted calls to run for re-election in 1992, setting a powerful precedent in a region where leaders frequently sought to cling to power. She peacefully handed the presidency to her elected successor, her former defense secretary Fidel Ramos, who had helped defend her government against coup plotters.
